title: Good-bye USD Dominance, Hello Again JPY
standfirst: The yen has been making a quiet comeback as a global currency. As a share of global FX reserves, its share rose from 3.4% in 2009 to 5.8% in 2025, despite the headwind of yen depreciation.

charts.title: The yen is making a comeback as a global currency
charts.ylabel: JPY share of world FX reserves, %
charts.note: Annual, year-end, at market exchange rates. 4.55% in 1980, a peak of 8.73% in 1991, then an almost uninterrupted slide to the 3.35% trough of 2009, and 5.84% in 2025. The recovery ran against the yen: it happened while the currency fell from about 120 to about 160 per dollar, which is why the report reads it as reserve managers buying rather than as a valuation effect.

charts.title: USD's slide from dominance through depreciation and quantity
charts.ylabel: USD share of world FX reserves, %
charts.note: 79.36% in 1975 to 56.42% in 2025. The two lines separate depreciation from reallocation and converge at 2025 by construction, since the constant-rate series is valued at end-2025 rates. The published chart marks the Plaza Accord of September 1985, after which the dollar lost about 35% against the yen in twelve months; the recent leg runs from the 64.67% of 2016, the highest reading of 2010-2025, to 56.42%.

charts.title: The euro's rise stalled after the euro crisis
charts.ylabel: EUR share of world FX reserves, %
charts.source: Sources: IMF, BIS, JMA estimates. Pre-1999 the euro line is the DEM+FRF+NLG composite at own rates.
charts.correction: The constant-rate value for 2019 reads 20.93 here. The library master shipped 19.82 — that year's observed share, overwritten when this chart was split out of majors_share_cer on 2026-08-05 — and that is the figure drawn in the PNG published with the post on the same day. Corrected in the master on 2026-08-05 after the cer-v4 build (20.90), the parent chart (20.93) and the standing reserves dataset (20.9) all disagreed with it; the parent's figure was restored because the master follows the parent's vintage in all 45 other comparable years. No figure the post prints in prose depends on it, and the 18.91-20.56 band it quotes is the observed series. These pages therefore draw the euro's constant-rate line correctly and the published image does not.
charts.note: The peak is 24.05% in 2009; over 2015-2025 the unadjusted share holds a 18.91-20.56% band. The single currency launched in January 1999, and the file starts in 1975 while the chart windows from 1980. Read the 1999 reading of 12.69% with care: the jump into 2000 is the IMF beginning to allocate its "currency unknown" bucket, not a market move, which is why the report's "18% at its debut" describes the early euro years rather than 1999 itself.

charts.title: Yen leads the diversification away from USD
charts.source: Sources: IMF, BIS, JMA estimates. CAD and AUD identified by the IMF from 2012, RMB from 2016.
charts.note: At market exchange rates. Three of the four series begin where the IMF first identifies them separately, and the gaps before those dates are left empty rather than filled. The RMB is the one line that has turned: 2.85% at its 2021 peak, 1.95% in 2025, now below both the Canadian dollar at 2.50% and the Australian at 2.02%. The yen at 5.84% is the largest of the four.

charts.title: Reserve managers consistently sold USD since 2010
charts.ylabel: pp of global FX reserves per year
charts.note: A flow, not a share: each bar is what reserve managers added to or shed from the dollar that year, in percentage points of global FX reserves, after the effect of exchange-rate moves is taken out. Thirteen of the sixteen years from 2010 are negative. 2022 is the clearest case — the dollar's appreciation alone would have lifted its share by 1.8 points, the share instead fell 0.5, and the difference of about 2.2 points is read as selling. The series starts in 1981 by ruling: the 1980 estimate spans an IMF Annual Report edition switch. Interest earned and reinvested stays inside these figures.
